source: Positions from SIMBAD (Wenger et al. 2000, A&AS 143, 9) except where the cited paper gives them; distances, redshifts and sizes from the papers cited with each object, or from the Gaia DR3 parallax where stated.

fields.nebulae: d in kpc; radiusDeg on the sky
fields.cosmos: z (redshift), or d in Mpc; size in kpc

map.name: UY Scuti

visit.ref: Radius 1,708 R☉ at 2.9 kpc (Arroyo-Torres et al. 2013), scaled to the Gaia distance; mass illustrative

map.note: One of the largest stars known: a red supergiant roughly 900 to 1,700 times the width of the Sun (its distance, and so its size, is uncertain). In the Sun’s place it would swallow the orbit of Mars.
map.ref: Arroyo-Torres et al. 2013, A&A 554, A76; distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax

map.name: Stephenson 2-18

visit.ref: Radius from its luminosity (4.4 × 10⁵ L☉) and temperature (3,200 K), Davies et al. 2007; mass illustrative

map.note: A red supergiant in the young cluster Stephenson 2, perhaps around 2,000 times the width of the Sun: a candidate for the largest star known.
map.ref: Davies et al. 2007, ApJ 671, 781 (position and the cluster’s distance)

map.name: Tabby’s Star
map.note: It dims by up to 22% at irregular times, far more than any planet could cause. The likeliest explanation is uneven clumps of fine dust.
map.ref: Boyajian et al. 2016, MNRAS 457, 3988; distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax

map.name: Przybylski’s Star
map.note: One of the strangest spectra of any star: rich in rare-earth elements such as holmium, with reported traces of short-lived heavy elements, and very little iron.
map.ref: Przybylski 1961, Nature 189, 739; Cowley et al. 2000, MNRAS 317, 299; distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax

map.name: Epsilon Aurigae
map.note: Every 27 years its light dips for nearly two years, as a companion wrapped in a huge, dark disc of dust passes in front of it.
map.ref: Kloppenborg et al. 2010, Nature 464, 870; distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax

map.name: WISE 0855−0714
map.note: The coldest brown dwarf known, at about −25 °C, and the fourth-nearest system to the Sun. It may have clouds of water ice.
map.ref: Luhman 2014, ApJL 786, L18; distance from its parallax (SIMBAD)

map.name: Scholz’s Star
map.note: About 70,000 years ago this pair passed roughly 52,000 AU from the Sun, through the outer Oort cloud: the closest known flyby of another star.
map.ref: Mamajek et al. 2015, ApJL 800, L17; distance from its parallax (SIMBAD)

map.name: SGR 1806−20
map.note: A magnetar: a neutron star with a magnetic field about a thousand trillion times Earth’s. Its giant flare of 27 December 2004 was the brightest burst from beyond the Solar System ever recorded, and it disturbed Earth’s upper atmosphere.
map.ref: Hurley et al. 2005, Nature 434, 1098; distance: Bibby et al. 2008, MNRAS 386, L23

map.name: Sagittarius Star Cloud (M24)
map.note: Messier 24: a gap in the dust that opens onto a dense field of stars in the Sagittarius Arm, about 10,000 light-years away.
map.ref: Messier 1764; distance of the Sagittarius Arm in this direction (Reid et al. 2019, ApJ 885, 131)

map.name: Winnecke 4 (M40)
map.note: Messier 40: two stars that only look close together. Messier listed it while hunting for a nebula reported in the area.
map.ref: Messier 1764; Gaia DR2 parallaxes (Gaia Collaboration 2018)

map.name: M73
map.note: Messier 73: four stars in a little Y that lie at different distances. A chance alignment, not a cluster.
map.ref: Odenkirchen & Soubiran 2002, A&A 383, 163

map.name: Smith Cloud
map.note: A comet-shaped cloud of hydrogen with at least a million suns’ worth of gas, falling into the Milky Way’s disc. It should strike in about 30 million years.
map.ref: Lockman et al. 2008, ApJL 679, L21

map.name: Eta Carinae
map.note: One of the most massive and luminous stars known: a binary whose main star holds around 100 times the Sun’s mass. In its “Great Eruption” of the 1840s it became the second-brightest star in the sky and threw off the Homunculus Nebula.
map.ref: Smith 2006, ApJ 644, 1151 (distance)

map.name: Rho Cassiopeiae
map.note: One of the rare yellow hypergiants, hundreds of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun. Every few decades it throws off a shell of gas and briefly fades.
map.ref: Lobel et al. 2003, ApJ 583, 923; distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax (uncertain)

map.name: Pistol Star
map.note: One of the most luminous stars in the Milky Way, near the Galactic Centre and hidden from the eye by dust. It has blown off the Pistol Nebula around itself.
map.ref: Figer et al. 1998, ApJ 506, 384

map.name: WR 104
map.note: A “pinwheel”: dust made where the winds of two massive stars collide is spun into a spiral by their eight-month orbit.
map.ref: Tuthill et al. 2008, ApJ 675, 698

map.name: Zeta Ophiuchi
map.note: A hot, fast-spinning star racing through space, probably flung free when its companion exploded; its wind ploughs a glowing bow shock ahead of it.
map.ref: Hoogerwerf et al. 2001, A&A 365, 49; distance from its parallax (SIMBAD)

map.name: RR Lyrae
map.note: The prototype of the RR Lyrae stars: old stars that pulse about every half day with a known luminosity, used as standard candles for globular clusters and nearby galaxies.
map.ref: Distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax

map.name: Chi Cygni
map.note: A Mira variable whose brightness swings by more than 10,000 times every 408 days, from easily seen to telescopic: the largest range of any star.
map.ref: Distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax

map.name: Hind’s Crimson Star
map.note: A carbon star so sooty that it glows a deep blood red, brightening and fading every 430 days or so.
map.ref: Hind 1845; distance from its Gaia DR3 parallax

map.name: Garnet Star
map.note: One of the largest and reddest stars visible to the naked eye. William Herschel called it “a very fine deep garnet colour”.
map.ref: Herschel 1783; distance of its association, Cep OB2 (Gaia)

map.name: Epsilon Lyrae
map.note: The “Double Double”: binoculars split it into two stars, and a telescope splits each of those into two again. All four are bound together.
map.ref: Hipparcos parallax (van Leeuwen 2007)

map.name: Arches Cluster
map.note: The densest young star cluster known in the Milky Way, about 100 light-years from the Galactic Centre and hidden behind dust. It holds dozens of the most massive stars known.
map.ref: Figer et al. 2002, ApJ 581, 258

map.name: Quintuplet Cluster
map.note: A massive young cluster near the Galactic Centre, named for five bright infrared sources. The Pistol Star is one of its members.
map.ref: Figer et al. 1999, ApJ 525, 750

map.name: Westerlund 1
map.note: The most massive young star cluster known in the Milky Way, tens of thousands of suns’ worth of stars, among them red supergiants and yellow hypergiants. Dust hides it from the eye.
map.ref: Clark et al. 2005, A&A 434, 949; distance from Gaia parallaxes (SIMBAD)

nebulae.name: Barnard’s Loop
nebulae.ref: Orion’s distance, Zucker et al. 2019, ApJ 879, 125

nebulae.name: Spaghetti Nebula (Simeis 147)
nebulae.ref: VLBI parallax of its pulsar PSR J0538+2817, Chatterjee et al. 2009, ApJ 698, 250

nebulae.name: Crescent Nebula
nebulae.ref: Gaia DR3 parallax of its star, WR 136

nebulae.name: Witch Head Nebula
nebulae.ref: Lit by Rigel: Hipparcos parallax, van Leeuwen 2007

nebulae.name: De Mairan’s Nebula (M43)
nebulae.ref: Orion Nebula Cluster, Menten et al. 2007, A&A 474, 515

nebulae.name: Pelican Nebula (IC 5070)
nebulae.ref: North America–Pelican complex, Kuhn et al. 2020, ApJ 899, 128

nebulae.name: Boomerang Nebula (the coldest known place, 1 K)
Pencil Nebula (NGC 2736)
nebulae.ref: Part of the Vela remnant, Dodson et al. 2003, ApJ 596, 1137

nebulae.name: Homunculus Nebula
nebulae.ref: Thrown off by Eta Carinae in the 1840s; Smith 2006, ApJ 644, 1151

nebulae.name: Sh2-106 (Celestial Snow Angel)
nebulae.ref: Distance of its molecular cloud (Zucker et al. 2020)

nebulae.name: Calabash Nebula (Rotten Egg)
nebulae.ref: In the open cluster M46 (Jura & Morris 1985)

sky.name: Kemble’s Cascade
sky.note: A straight chain of about 20 stars, 2.5° long, ending at the small cluster NGC 1502. Named after Father Lucian Kemble; the stars lie at different distances.

sky.name: Coathanger (Collinder 399)
sky.note: Ten stars that make an upside-down coat hanger. Gaia shows they lie at different distances: a chance alignment, not a cluster.

cosmos.name: M59
cosmos.label: Elliptical galaxy
cosmos.note: Messier 59: one of the giant elliptical galaxies of the Virgo Cluster.
cosmos.ref: Virgo Cluster’s distance: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144

cosmos.name: M85
cosmos.label: Lenticular galaxy
cosmos.note: Messier 85: the northernmost big galaxy of the Virgo Cluster, with young stars at its centre left by a merger a few billion years ago.
cosmos.ref: Virgo Cluster’s distance: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144

cosmos.name: M86
cosmos.label: Elliptical galaxy
cosmos.note: A giant elliptical galaxy falling through the Virgo Cluster so fast that it is coming towards us, at about 240 km/s: one of the few galaxies with a blueshift.
cosmos.ref: Virgo Cluster’s distance: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144

cosmos.name: M89
cosmos.label: Elliptical galaxy
cosmos.note: An almost perfectly round elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, wrapped in faint shells and plumes of stars left by past mergers.
cosmos.ref: Virgo Cluster’s distance: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144

cosmos.name: M90
cosmos.label: Spiral galaxy
cosmos.note: A spiral galaxy of the Virgo Cluster coming towards us. The cluster’s hot gas is stripping away the gas it needs to make new stars.
cosmos.ref: Virgo Cluster’s distance: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144

cosmos.name: M91
cosmos.label: Barred spiral galaxy
cosmos.note: A barred spiral in the Virgo Cluster. For two centuries it was Messier’s “missing” object, because he wrote down its position wrongly.
cosmos.ref: Virgo Cluster’s distance: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144

cosmos.name: M98
cosmos.label: Spiral galaxy
cosmos.note: A spiral galaxy seen nearly edge-on in the Virgo Cluster, coming towards us at about 140 km/s.
cosmos.ref: Virgo Cluster’s distance: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144

cosmos.name: Spindle Galaxy (M102)
cosmos.label: Lenticular galaxy, edge-on
cosmos.note: Usually taken to be Messier 102 (his own record is ambiguous): a lenticular galaxy seen edge-on, cut by a sharp, thin lane of dust.

cosmos.name: Hoag’s Object
cosmos.label: Ring galaxy
cosmos.note: A nearly perfect ring of young blue stars around an old yellow core, with a dark gap between them. How it formed is still debated.
cosmos.ref: Hoag 1950, AJ 55, 170; Schweizer et al. 1987, ApJ 320, 454

cosmos.name: Malin 1
cosmos.label: Giant low-surface-brightness spiral
cosmos.note: One of the largest disc galaxies known: its faint spiral disc spans several hundred thousand light-years, several times the Milky Way.
cosmos.ref: Bothun et al. 1987, AJ 94, 23; Galaz et al. 2015, ApJL 815, L29

cosmos.name: IC 1101
cosmos.label: Supergiant elliptical galaxy
cosmos.note: The central galaxy of the cluster Abell 2029, one of the largest galaxies known, with the largest core of stars ever measured, scoured out by its giant black hole.

cosmos.name: Dragonfly 44
cosmos.label: Ultra-diffuse galaxy
cosmos.note: An ultra-diffuse galaxy in the Coma Cluster, nearly as wide as the Milky Way but with about 1% of its stars: almost all of its mass is dark matter.
cosmos.ref: van Dokkum et al. 2016, ApJL 828, L6 (position and redshift)

cosmos.name: Cartwheel Galaxy
cosmos.label: Ring galaxy
cosmos.note: A smaller galaxy plunged through its disc a few hundred million years ago, sending a ring of new stars rippling outward like a stone dropped in a pond.

cosmos.name: Stephan’s Quintet
cosmos.label: Compact group of galaxies
cosmos.note: Four galaxies locked in a slow collision about 290 million light-years away. The fifth, NGC 7320, only lines up with them: it is several times closer.

cosmos.name: Crater II
cosmos.label: Dwarf galaxy (satellite of the Milky Way)
cosmos.note: One of the Milky Way’s largest satellite galaxies, yet so faint and spread out that it was only found in 2016: one of the most diffuse galaxies known.

cosmos.name: Antlia II
cosmos.label: Dwarf galaxy (satellite of the Milky Way)
cosmos.note: A ghostly dwarf galaxy hidden behind the Milky Way’s disc, found with Gaia in 2018: about as large as the Large Magellanic Cloud, yet thousands of times fainter.

cosmos.name: El Gordo
cosmos.label: Colliding galaxy clusters
cosmos.note: “The Fat One”: two galaxy clusters in collision, the most massive cluster known from when the universe was half its present age.

cosmos.name: Phoenix Cluster
cosmos.label: Galaxy cluster
cosmos.note: Its central galaxy forms several hundred new suns a year, hundreds of times the Milky Way’s rate, fed by gas cooling out of the cluster.

cosmos.name: Einstein Cross
cosmos.label: Gravitationally lensed quasar
cosmos.note: A quasar seen as four images around the core of a much nearer galaxy (redshift 0.04), whose gravity bends its light: a gravitational lens, as Einstein predicted.

cosmos.name: Mayall’s Object
cosmos.label: Colliding galaxies (ring and tail)
cosmos.note: Two galaxies just after a head-on collision: one has become a ring, the other is stretched into a tail, so the pair looks like a ring on a stalk.

cosmos.name: I Zwicky 18
cosmos.label: Blue compact dwarf galaxy
cosmos.note: One of the most metal-poor galaxies known, almost as pristine as galaxies in the early universe, yet only 59 million light-years away and still forming stars.

cosmos.name: Canis Major Dwarf Galaxy
cosmos.label: Dwarf galaxy (disputed)
cosmos.note: Claimed in 2003 as the Milky Way’s nearest satellite galaxy, 25,000 light-years from the Sun and being torn apart. It may instead be part of the Milky Way’s warped outer disc.

cosmos.name: Markarian 421
cosmos.label: Blazar (BL Lac object)
cosmos.note: One of the nearest blazars: a galaxy whose jet points almost straight at us, one of the first sources of very-high-energy (TeV) gamma rays found beyond the Milky Way.

cosmos.name: Hercules A
cosmos.label: Radio galaxy
cosmos.note: A giant elliptical galaxy whose black hole blows jets more than a million light-years long: one of the brightest radio sources in the sky.

cosmos.name: Comet Galaxy
cosmos.label: Spiral galaxy being stripped
cosmos.note: A spiral galaxy falling into the cluster Abell 2667 so fast that the cluster’s gas strips it, leaving a tail of gas and new stars hundreds of thousands of light-years long.
cosmos.ref: Cortese et al. 2007, MNRAS 376, 157 (position: its cluster, Abell 2667)

cosmos.name: MACS0647-JD
cosmos.label: Early galaxy, seen through a gravitational lens
cosmos.note: One of the most distant galaxies known, seen about 460 million years after the Big Bang and magnified by a galaxy cluster. Webb showed it is two clumps.
cosmos.ref: Coe et al. 2013, ApJ 762, 32 (position); Hsiao et al. 2023 (redshift)

cosmos.name: CR7
cosmos.label: Early galaxy
cosmos.note: One of the brightest galaxies of the early universe, 800 million years after the Big Bang. Its unusual light once suggested the very first generation of stars.

cosmos.name: Abell S1063
cosmos.label: Galaxy cluster (gravitational lens)
cosmos.note: A massive cluster whose gravity magnifies the galaxies far behind it: one of Hubble’s Frontier Fields.

cosmos.name: MACS J0717
cosmos.label: Merging galaxy clusters
cosmos.note: Four galaxy clusters colliding, fed by a long filament of matter: one of the most complex cluster mergers known, and a Hubble Frontier Field.
cosmos.ref: Ebeling et al. 2004, ApJL 609, L49; Lotz et al. 2017

cosmos.name: Earendel
cosmos.label: Single star, seen through a gravitational lens
cosmos.note: The most distant single star ever seen. Its light, from about 900 million years after the Big Bang, is magnified thousands of times by a galaxy cluster in front.
cosmos.ref: Welch et al. 2022, Nature 603, 815 (position and redshift)
